    A culture grows continuously. Two measurements are taken: P(0)=60P(0)=60P(0)=60 cells and P(12)=90P(12)=90P(12)=90 cells, twelve hours later. This question infers the continuous growth rate from those two readings, then compares it to the EFFECTIVE per-hour rate a once-per-hour (discrete, compounded hourly) schedule would need to match the same two readings exactly.

    1. A
      Part A.

      Use the two measurements to find the continuous growth rate rrr (as a percent, to three decimal places), using the model P(t)=P(0)ertP(t)=P(0)e^{rt}P(t)=P(0)ert.

      Solve and show your work Write each step out, and end with the value and its units. 4 points

    2. B
      Part B.

      A discrete, once-per-hour compounding schedule D(t)=D(0)(1+i)tD(t)=D(0)(1+i)^{t}D(t)=D(0)(1+i)t (ttt in whole hours) is required to match the SAME two readings, D(0)=60D(0)=60D(0)=60 and D(12)=90D(12)=90D(12)=90. Find the effective hourly rate iii (as a percent, to three decimal places), and state which rate is larger, rrr or iii, without yet explaining why.

      Carry your own answer forward Compare your value of iii to your own value of rrr from part A.

      Solve and show your work Write each step out, and end with the value and its units. 4 points

    3. C
      Part C.

      Explain, in general (not just for these two specific numbers), why the discrete effective rate iii needed to match a continuous rate rrr over the SAME elapsed time must always be larger than rrr itself, tying your answer to the inequality ex>1+xe^{x} > 1+xex>1+x for every x>0x>0x>0.

      Justify your claim State the claim, then give the reason it has to be true. 4 points

    The answer

    Part A

    r≈0.03379r\approx0.03379r≈0.03379, about 3.379%3.379\%3.379% per hour.

    Part B

    i≈0.03437i\approx0.03437i≈0.03437, about 3.437%3.437\%3.437% per hour; i>ri>ri>r.

    Part C

    Matching the two schedules exactly requires 1+i=er1+i=e^{r}1+i=er (same per-hour growth factor). Since ex>1+xe^{x}>1+xex>1+x for every x>0x>0x>0, setting x=rx=rx=r gives er>1+re^{r}>1+rer>1+r, so i=er−1>ri=e^{r}-1>ri=er−1>r: the discrete effective rate must always exceed the continuous rate.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    P(12)=P(0)e12r  ⟹  90=60e12r  ⟹  e12r=1.5  ⟹  12r=ln⁡1.5≈0.405465  ⟹  r≈0.033789P(12)=P(0)e^{12r} \;\Longrightarrow\; 90=60e^{12r} \;\Longrightarrow\; e^{12r}=1.5 \;\Longrightarrow\; 12r=\ln1.5\approx0.405465 \;\Longrightarrow\; r\approx0.033789P(12)=P(0)e12r⟹90=60e12r⟹e12r=1.5⟹12r=ln1.5≈0.405465⟹r≈0.033789

    So the continuous rate is about 3.379%3.379\%3.379% per hour.

    Part B

    D(12)=D(0)(1+i)12  ⟹  90=60(1+i)12  ⟹  (1+i)12=1.5  ⟹  1+i=1.51/12≈1.034366  ⟹  i≈0.034366D(12)=D(0)(1+i)^{12} \;\Longrightarrow\; 90=60(1+i)^{12} \;\Longrightarrow\; (1+i)^{12}=1.5 \;\Longrightarrow\; 1+i=1.5^{1/12}\approx1.034366 \;\Longrightarrow\; i\approx0.034366D(12)=D(0)(1+i)12⟹90=60(1+i)12⟹(1+i)12=1.5⟹1+i=1.51/12≈1.034366⟹i≈0.034366

    So the effective hourly rate is about 3.437%3.437\%3.437%, which is LARGER than the continuous rate r≈3.379%r\approx3.379\%r≈3.379% found in part A.

    Part C

    For the discrete schedule to reproduce the SAME values as the continuous one at every hour, not just at t=12t=12t=12, the two per-hour growth factors must match exactly:

    1+i=er.1+i = e^{r}.1+i=er.

    Now apply the given inequality ex>1+xe^{x}>1+xex>1+x, valid for every x>0x>0x>0, with x=rx=rx=r (since r>0r>0r>0 for a growing quantity):

    er>1+r.e^{r} > 1+r.er>1+r.

    Substituting 1+i=er1+i=e^{r}1+i=er into this inequality,

    1+i>1+r  ⟹  i>r.1+i > 1+r \;\Longrightarrow\; i > r.1+i>1+r⟹i>r.

    So the discrete effective rate is always strictly larger than the continuous rate needed to match it, for ANY positive rrr, not only the 3.379%3.379\%3.379% found in part A. Continuous compounding is more efficient at turning a given per-hour rate into growth, so a discrete schedule needs a boosted rate to keep pace.

    In one line

    The continuous rate is r≈3.379%r\approx3.379\%r≈3.379% per hour (from e12r=1.5e^{12r}=1.5e12r=1.5); the equivalent discrete hourly rate is i≈3.437%i\approx3.437\%i≈3.437% (from (1+i)12=1.5(1+i)^{12}=1.5(1+i)12=1.5), so i>ri>ri>r; and in general, matching requires 1+i=er1+i=e^{r}1+i=er, and since er>1+re^{r}>1+rer>1+r for every r>0r>0r>0, it follows that i=er−1>ri=e^{r}-1>ri=er−1>r always, meaning a discrete schedule always needs a higher stated rate than an equivalent continuous one.

    10. A budget that multiplies against one that only grows by degree . 11 points. Question 10 of 10.

    11 pts

    Let f(x)=3xf(x) = 3^{x}f(x)=3x and q(x)=x5q(x) = x^{5}q(x)=x5.

    1. A
      Part A.

      Evaluate fff and qqq at x=5x=5x=5 and x=6x=6x=6, and state which function is larger at each input.

      Solve and show your work Write each step out, and end with the value and its units. 3 points

    2. B
      Part B.

      Without computing further values, explain why fff must EVENTUALLY overtake qqq permanently, even though qqq is ahead at both inputs checked in part A, using the fact that fff's per-step growth factor is fixed while qqq's is not.

      Explain why it works A sentence or two. Reasons, not steps. 4 points

    3. C
      Part C.

      Now consider a second exponential, h(x)=1.2xh(x)=1.2^{x}h(x)=1.2x, racing against the SAME polynomial q(x)=x5q(x)=x^{5}q(x)=x5. Without evaluating any specific values of hhh or qqq, explain whether hhh must ALSO eventually overtake qqq permanently, and explain whether hhh's crossover point should happen sooner or later than fff's crossover point found in parts A and B, using only the sizes of the two bases 1.21.21.2 and 333.

      Explain why it works A sentence or two. Reasons, not steps. 4 points

    The answer

    Part A

    f(5)=243<q(5)=3125f(5)=243<q(5)=3125f(5)=243<q(5)=3125; f(6)=729<q(6)=7776f(6)=729<q(6)=7776f(6)=729<q(6)=7776; qqq leads at both.

    Part B

    fff's per-step factor is fixed forever at 333, while qqq's per-step factor (x+1x)5\left(\tfrac{x+1}{x}\right)^{5}(xx+1​)5 shrinks toward 111 as xxx grows; a fixed factor must eventually exceed a shrinking one, and once it does, the lead never returns.

    Part C

    Yes, hhh must also eventually overtake qqq permanently, since its base 1.2>11.2>11.2>1 gives a fixed per-step factor forever, exactly like fff; but because 1.21.21.2 is much closer to 111 than 333 is, qqq's shrinking factor takes longer to drop below 1.21.21.2 than below 333, so hhh's crossover happens later than fff's.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    f(5)=35=243, q(5)=55=3125;f(6)=36=729, q(6)=65=7776f(5)=3^{5}=243,\ q(5)=5^{5}=3125; \qquad f(6)=3^{6}=729,\ q(6)=6^{5}=7776f(5)=35=243, q(5)=55=3125;f(6)=36=729, q(6)=65=7776

    At both inputs qqq is larger: 243<3125243<3125243<3125 and 729<7776729<7776729<7776.

    Part B

    Every step of fff multiplies by the same fixed factor 333, forever, since f(x+1)/f(x)=3f(x+1)/f(x)=3f(x+1)/f(x)=3 for every xxx. The step factor of qqq shrinks toward 111 as xxx grows, since 1x\dfrac1xx1​ shrinks.

    f(x+1)f(x)=3 (fixed),q(x+1)q(x)=(x+1x)5⟶1 as x→∞\frac{f(x+1)}{f(x)}=3 \text{ (fixed)}, \qquad \frac{q(x+1)}{q(x)}=\left(\frac{x+1}{x}\right)^{5} \longrightarrow 1 \text{ as } x\to\inftyf(x)f(x+1)​=3 (fixed),q(x)q(x+1)​=(xx+1​)5⟶1 as x→∞

    A fixed number greater than 111 and a quantity shrinking toward 111 must eventually cross, so there is some point past which fff's fixed step beats qqq's shrinking step at every later input. Once fff takes the lead, every further step multiplies it by more than qqq is multiplied by, so the gap only grows and the lead can never pass back.

    Part C

    Every exponential with base greater than 111 keeps a fixed per-step growth factor forever; that part of the earlier argument has nothing to do with which particular base is racing against qqq, so it applies to hhh exactly as it applied to fff. Since 1.2>11.2>11.2>1, hhh has a fixed factor of 1.21.21.2 forever, and qqq's per-step factor still shrinks toward 111 as xxx grows, regardless of which exponential it is being compared to. A fixed factor greater than 111 must still eventually exceed a factor shrinking toward 111, so hhh permanently overtakes qqq as well, by the identical reasoning.

    The two crossovers happen at different places, though. Starting out large, qqq's per-step factor decreases toward 111 as xxx grows. It only has to shrink down past 333 for fff to take the lead, but it must shrink much further, down past the smaller number 1.21.21.2, for hhh to take the lead. Since qqq's factor is heading toward 111 from above and 1.21.21.2 sits much closer to 111 than 333 does, qqq's factor reaches the neighborhood of 333 well before it reaches the neighborhood of 1.21.21.2. So hhh's crossover happens LATER than fff's: a base closer to 111 still wins eventually, but it takes longer to do so.

    q(x+1)/q(x)→1 from above; crosses below 3 before it crosses below 1.2⟹xf-crossover<xh-crossoverq(x+1)/q(x) \to 1 \text{ from above; crosses below } 3 \text{ before it crosses below } 1.2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad x_{f\text{-crossover}} < x_{h\text{-crossover}}q(x+1)/q(x)→1 from above; crosses below 3 before it crosses below 1.2⟹xf-crossover​<xh-crossover​

    In one line

    qqq leads at x=5x=5x=5 (3125>2433125>2433125>243) and x=6x=6x=6 (7776>7297776>7297776>729), but fff must eventually overtake qqq permanently, because fff's per-step factor stays fixed at 333 forever while qqq's per-step factor shrinks toward 111; a second exponential h(x)=1.2xh(x)=1.2^{x}h(x)=1.2x must also eventually overtake qqq permanently, by the same argument, but since 1.21.21.2 is much closer to 111 than 333 is, qqq's shrinking per-step factor takes longer to drop below 1.21.21.2 than below 333, so hhh's crossover happens later than fff's.
